turns: "A new study finds that getting pregnant after a woman gets her tubes tied—colloquial for permanent female surgical sterilization—may be more common than previously assumed. Published in the New England Journal of Medicine Evidence, the study examined survey data of more than 4,000 women who reported tubal ligations. Tubal ligation is the formal term for a range of surgeries that clamp or remove fallopian tubes. Researchers found that 3-5% of these women reported pregnancy after surgery. Dr. Eleanor Bimla Schwarz, an internist at UC San Francisco and lead researcher, noted that tubal sterilization is an important form of contraception. She emphasized that every form of contraception fails at some point, so we need to know about alternatives that are effective. She also stated that we need to accept that abortion services will always be needed because even highly effective methods do fail. The study is especially relevant since the US Supreme Court overturned Roe v Wade in 2022. Dozens of states have since banned and severely restricted abortion access. Research has found that interest in permanent female surgical sterilization has increased among women aged 18-30. Researchers conducted the study by analyzing data from four iterations of the US National Survey of Family Growth spanning 2002 to 2015. Of the 31,000 women covered in the survey, 4,184 reported tubal ligation. In those surveys, between 3 and 5% of women reported pregnancy after surgery. The findings underscore that permanent sterilization, while effective, is not infallible and carries a small but non-trivial risk of pregnancy. P.P.S The findings of this study are particularly important in the current political landscape where access to contraception and reproductive options remains a central topic of public discourse and policy debate."
